retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach locates all wisdom with the Lord; Proverbs likewise names the Lord as giver of wisdom and the source of knowledge and understanding.
Sirach asks who can count rain and other quantities beyond human reckoning; God's question in Job asks who counts clouds with wisdom. Both challenge human mastery of the heavens' quantities.

Sirach links inaccessible cosmic dimensions with wisdom. The speech in Job likewise challenges human understanding through heaven's height, depths, and the earth and sea's extent; its accusation against Job is not endorsed here.

Wisdom's creation before all things corresponds to personified Wisdom's account of being created before earth, depths and mountains in Proverbs. The shared claim concerns wisdom's priority in creation.
Sirach asks to whom wisdom's root was revealed; Job asks where wisdom is found, says it escapes human sight, and contrasts this with God's knowledge of its place.
Sirach identifies One who is wise, subsequently named as the Lord; Romans' doxology praises the only wise God. The connection concerns divine wisdom, without adding throne imagery to Romans.
Sirach describes God seeing and ordering wisdom before pouring her upon His works; Job likewise describes Him seeing, preparing and tracing out wisdom within His ordering of creation.
Wisdom is supplied according to God's giving in Sirach; James directs those lacking wisdom to the God who gives generously. Both locate the gift's availability in God.
Sirach associates fear of the Lord with rejoicing; the psalm calls those fearing the Lord happy and promises their well-being. Reverence and happiness are joined in both.
Sirach promises length of days through fear of the Lord; Proverbs explicitly says that fear of the Lord adds days. The longevity promise closely corresponds.
Sirach says the Lord-fearing person's end will be good; Ecclesiastes affirms that it will be good for those fearing God despite the sinner's apparent prolongation.
Both verses explicitly identify fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom. Sirach's additional womb imagery is not attributed to Proverbs.
Wisdom is trusted among people's offspring in Sirach 1; chapter 4 explains her possession as an inheritance held by descendants. Both describe wisdom continuing across generations.
Wisdom intoxicates with her fruits in chapter 1; in chapter 24 she invites people to eat her produce and drink. Both portray participation in wisdom through consumption imagery.
Sirach's wisdom fills a house and storehouses with desirable produce; Proverbs joins a house built through wisdom to store-rooms filled with precious wealth through discernment.
Sirach connects fear of the Lord with healing health; Proverbs connects fearing God and avoiding evil with healing for body and bones. Both describe reverence through bodily well-being.
Sirach's divine seeing and distribution of wisdom corresponds to Job's account of God seeing, preparing and expounding wisdom. Job's wording is not represented as an identical counting formula.
Sirach pictures long days as branches growing from fear of the Lord; Proverbs states directly that fear of the Lord adds days. The image develops the same longevity teaching.
Sirach denies justification to unjust anger; James says human anger does not accomplish God's righteousness. Both reject anger as a reliable means of right conduct.
Sirach promises gladness after patient endurance; James calls those who endure blessed and invokes Job's outcome from the compassionate Lord. Both look beyond present hardship.
Sirach's wise person conceals words until the right time; Proverbs commends withholding a harsh word and associates silence with intelligence. Speech restraint displays discernment in both.
Sirach contrasts wisdom's knowledge with the sinner's aversion to reverence; Proverbs joins reverence with perception and says the ungodly despise wisdom and discipline.
Sirach tells wisdom-seekers to keep commandments; the psalm joins fear of the Lord with wisdom and good understanding for those who practice it. Both connect understanding with obedient practice.

Sirach associates wisdom with faithfulness and gentleness pleasing to God; James describes wisdom from above as peaceable, considerate and merciful. Both describe wisdom through conduct toward others.
Sirach forbids approaching God with a divided heart; James commands those of divided mind to purify their hearts as they draw near to God.

Sirach forbids hypocritical conduct in people's speech; Jesus condemns an outward appearance of righteousness concealing inward hypocrisy. Both reject a deceptive public presentation of one's character.
Sirach warns that self-exaltation ends in humiliation before the assembly; Jesus' banquet parable depicts shame before fellow guests and concludes that self-exalters will be humbled.
Sirach prepares a new servant of the Lord for testing; James tells believers to expect trials that test faith and produce endurance. Testing belongs within faithful life in both.
Sirach commands a steady heart and endurance in calamity; the psalm tells the waiting worshipper to act courageously and let the heart be strong while waiting for the Lord.
Sirach's instruction to cling to the Lord without withdrawing closely corresponds to Deuteronomy's combined commands to fear, serve and cleave to Him.

Sirach calls for patience in humiliation; Hebrews urges endurance of painful discipline for its later benefit. The comparison concerns patient reception of hardship, without identifying every adversity as the same event.

Sirach compares acceptable people tested in humiliation with gold tested in fire; Peter likewise compares faith tested through trials with fire-tested gold. Both use refining to explain human testing.
Sirach combines trust in God with setting one's ways straight; Proverbs commands wholehearted trust in God and attendance to wisdom for straight paths, rather than self-reliance.
Sirach addresses those fearing the Lord and waiting for mercy; the psalm describes precisely those who fear Him, hope in His mercy and wait for His help.
Sirach assures the Lord-fearing that trust will not lose its reward; the psalm declares that those waiting for God will not be put to shame. Both oppose trust to final disappointment.
Sirach urges hope for gladness and mercy; Romans asks the God of hope to fill believers with joy and peace so that hope abounds. Both join reliance on God with joy.
Sirach asks whether earlier generations trusted and were ashamed or called without response; the psalm says the fathers hoped, cried to God, were rescued and were not ashamed.
Sirach explains trust through the Lord's compassion and forgiveness; the psalm calls Him compassionate and merciful and says He has not repaid people according to their sins.
Sirach condemns a sinner walking two paths; James describes the person of divided mind as unstable in all his ways. Both use divided direction to depict failed trust.
Sirach's slack heart lacks trust and shelter; Hebrews contrasts faithful preservation of the soul with drawing back to destruction. The warnings connect abandoned trust with peril.
Sirach warns those who lose endurance before the Lord's visitation; Hebrews urges endurance to receive the promise and warns against drawing back while awaiting the coming One.
Sirach identifies love for the Lord with keeping His ways; Jesus identifies the person keeping His commandments as the one who loves Him. Both make obedience the expression of love.

Sirach says those loving the Lord are filled with the law; the psalm's speaker loves, meditates on and raises his hands toward God's commandments. Both depict affectionate engagement with divine instruction.
Sirach's preparation of hearts and humbling of souls corresponds to James' commands to purify hearts and humble oneself before the Lord.
Sirach prefers falling into the Lord's hands because of His mercy; David likewise chooses the Lord's hand rather than human hands because His compassions are many.
Sirach addresses children as a father asking them to listen and act; Proverbs likewise calls children to hear a father's discipline and retain his teaching.
Sirach grounds parental honor and authority in the Lord; Exodus commands honor for both father and mother. Both present parental honor as a divine obligation.
Honoring a father is connected with atonement here; verse 14 develops this through mercy toward a father being remembered in place of sins. The two statements frame filial care's moral significance.

The mother's honor is valued like stored treasure here; chapter 7 commands remembrance of her labor pains and asks what repayment could match the parents' gift. Both stress the weight of filial gratitude.
Sirach promises long days to one glorifying a father; Exodus attaches long days and well-being to honoring father and mother. The stated benefit closely corresponds.
Sirach describes service to those who brought one into being; Colossians tells children to obey parents because this pleases the Lord. Both connect filial obedience with religious duty.
Sirach commands honor in deeds and words in hope of a father's blessing; Exodus likewise commands parental honor and attaches a promise of well-being. The promised benefits are expressed differently.

Sirach describes a father's blessing establishing his children's houses; Isaac's blessing grants abundance and familial authority to Jacob. This illustrates the blessing's substance without commending Jacob's deceptive means of receiving it.
Sirach denies glory to one who glories in a father's dishonor; Proverbs says dishonoring a father and expelling a mother brings shame and reproach upon the child.
Sirach says a person's glory comes from a father's honor; Proverbs calls fathers the boast of their children. Both connect children's standing with parental honor.
Sirach commands support for an aging father; Jesus condemns a religious practice that prevents children providing benefits to father or mother. Both require parental honor to include practical help.
Sirach forbids dishonoring a father who loses understanding; Proverbs forbids despising a mother because she is old. Both reject age or loss of understanding as grounds for disrespect.
Mercy toward a father being remembered in place of sins develops verse 3's claim that honoring a father atones for sins. The repeated theme connects honor with concrete care.
Sirach promises remembrance in affliction after filial mercy; chapter 29 pictures stored almsgiving rescuing its giver from affliction. Both connect prior mercy with help in later distress.

Sirach condemns abandonment of a father and provocation of a mother; Exodus imposes death for reviling either parent. Both treat assault upon parental honor as a grave offense, while naming different actions.
Sirach commands greater humility as one's greatness increases and promises divine favor; James contrasts God's opposition to the proud with grace given to the humble.

retained_triples_independently_read.relationship: The high Lord and the humble
retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach joins the Lord's great dominion with His glorification by the humble; the psalm says the high Lord watches the lowly and knows the lofty from afar.

Sirach warns against investigating what exceeds one's strength; the psalm's humble speaker refuses to walk among great matters or wonders beyond him. Both express humility through restraint of ambition.
Sirach directs attention to commanded duties instead of hidden matters; Deuteronomy reserves hidden things to God and gives revealed things to the people for doing the law.
This warning against matters beyond one's tasks continues verses 21–22's distinction between excessive inquiry and commanded duties. The sequence clarifies the practical boundary being urged.
Sirach warns that assumptions and bad suspicion mislead thought; Proverbs describes a seemingly upright way whose outcome is Hades. Both warn that apparent rightness can conceal dangerous error.
Sirach predicts harm for a hard heart; Proverbs likewise says the hard-hearted person will fall into evils. The shared warning opposes unyielding confidence.
Sirach connects a hard heart with added sins and troubles; Romans says hardness and an unrepentant heart store up wrath for judgment. Both portray persistence in sin as accumulating consequences.
Sirach says the proud person's calamity has no healing; Proverbs describes a stiff-necked person's sudden burning with no healing. Both associate obstinate pride with irreversible ruin.
Sirach commends an understanding heart considering a proverb and a listening ear; Proverbs describes a wise listener becoming wiser and understanding comparisons, obscure sayings and riddles.
Sirach says almsgiving atones for sins; Daniel urges the king to redeem injustices by almsgiving. Both explicitly connect merciful giving with addressing wrongdoing.

Sirach links repaying favors with future support; Jesus' exhortation to give promises a measure given back. Both connect generous action with subsequent benefit, without requiring identical circumstances of repayment.
Sirach forbids depriving poor people of livelihood or delaying them; Deuteronomy forbids closing the hand to a needy brother and commands assistance according to his need.
Sirach forbids grieving a hungry, helpless person; Proverbs condemns mocking the poor as provocation of their Maker and commends compassion instead.
Sirach forbids delaying a gift to someone in need; Proverbs forbids telling a needy person to return tomorrow when help can be given now.
Sirach prohibits rejecting the afflicted supplicant; Deuteronomy prohibits withholding affection and closing the hand against a needy brother. Both command a receptive response to need.
Sirach forbids turning one's eye from the needy; Proverbs contrasts giving to the poor with turning away one's eye and encountering great difficulty. Both warn against deliberate refusal to see need.
Sirach warns that the poor person's Maker hears his bitter petition; Exodus says God hears the cry of afflicted widows and orphans and responds against their oppressors.

Sirach counsels respectful bearing before a person of high rank; Romans commands honor where honor is due within its discussion of governing authorities. Both address conduct toward recognized authority.

Sirach requires a peaceable, gentle answer to the poor; Proverbs says a yielding answer turns away wrath whereas a painful word arouses it. The poor person's dignity is Sirach's particular application.
Sirach commands rescue from a wrongdoer's hand and courage in judgment; the psalm commands judgment for the vulnerable and rescue from a sinner's hand.
Sirach calls for fatherly care of orphans and support for their mother; Job recalls helping an orphan, receiving a widow's blessing, and acting as father to the powerless.
Sirach's wisdom takes hold of those seeking her; personified Wisdom in Proverbs promises that those seeking her will find her. Both portray a responsive encounter with wisdom.
Sirach equates love of wisdom with love of life; Proverbs' Wisdom describes her ways as ways to life and divine favor. Both present life as wisdom's benefit.
Sirach promises glory to the one holding wisdom fast; Proverbs urges honoring her and says she will exalt, embrace and crown the learner. Both describe wisdom rewarding attachment with honor.

Sirach says the Lord loves those loving wisdom; Wisdom of Solomon restricts God's love to those dwelling with wisdom. Both connect divine love with a person's relationship to wisdom, using different logical formulations.
Sirach says one obeying wisdom will judge nations; Proverbs' Wisdom claims that kings and rulers govern through her. Both locate sound public authority in wisdom.
Wisdom becomes an inheritance held by descendants here; chapter 1 describes her as trusted among offspring. Both picture wisdom enduring within successive generations.

Wisdom initially frightens and disciplines her pupil in Sirach; Hebrews describes discipline as presently sorrowful but later fruitful. Both distinguish training's initial pain from its later benefit.
After testing, wisdom gladdens and reveals hidden things here; chapter 6 promises that seeking her leads to finding her rest and gladness. Both describe her reward after persevering pursuit.
Sirach warns that straying causes wisdom to abandon a person to downfall; Proverbs' Wisdom refuses those who rejected her counsel when their destruction arrives.

retained_triples_independently_read.relationship: Wise attention to time and evil
retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach commands watchfulness for the right time and protection against evil; Ephesians joins careful wise conduct with taking the opportunity because the days are evil.
Sirach distinguishes shame leading to sin from shame bringing honor; chapter 41 explicitly warns that not every kind of shame should be preserved. The later instruction develops that distinction.
Sirach forbids harmful deference to persons; Proverbs declares showing deference to a face in judgment wrong and condemns acquitting the impious. Both subordinate personal regard to right judgment.
Sirach commands speaking when needed; Proverbs describes the evil person's failure to say something timely and good for the community. The negative portrait contrasts with Sirach's positive duty.
Sirach says wisdom becomes known through speech; Proverbs describes a wise heart understanding its mouth's utterance and carrying discernment upon the lips.
Sirach forbids speaking against truth; Ephesians commands putting away falsehood and speaking truth with one's neighbor. Both make truth a governing rule for speech.
Sirach forbids shame from preventing confession; First John promises forgiveness and cleansing when sins are confessed. Both commend acknowledged wrongdoing instead of its concealment.
Sirach forbids deference to someone powerful; James condemns giving preferential treatment to a richly dressed person over a poor visitor. Both reject rank-based partiality.

retained_triples_independently_read.relationship: Fidelity at the cost of death
retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach urges struggle for truth until death with God's help; the Maccabean speaker gives body and soul for ancestral laws while appealing for God's mercy. This is an ethical comparison, not an asserted quotation.
Sirach contrasts rash speech with slack deeds; James commands slowness to speak and then becoming doers rather than merely hearers of the word.
Sirach forbids lion-like conduct in one's household toward slaves; Ephesians instructs masters to give up threats because they themselves have a heavenly Master.
Sirach condemns a hand open to receive but closed when repaying; chapter 29 expressly commands repayment at the appointed time and faithfulness to one's word.
Sirach forbids declaring possessions sufficient; Jesus' rich man tells his soul its stored goods ensure ease, only to have his life demanded that night.
Sirach warns against following one's soul and strength in the heart's desires; Numbers directs remembrance of God's commandments instead of turning aside after one's thoughts and eyes.
Sirach rejects the boast that no one has power over the speaker; the psalm reports boastful speakers claiming their lips as their own and asking who is their lord.
Sirach rejects the sinner's claim that nothing happened after sin; Ecclesiastes says lack of prompt contradiction emboldens people to do evil. Both expose a false inference from apparent impunity.
Sirach forbids adding sins through careless confidence about atonement; Romans rejects remaining in sin so that grace may increase. Both oppose using divine pardon as permission to continue sinning.
Sirach warns against assuming great compassion cancels continued sin; Romans says God's patience calls for repentance and warns that hard-heartedness stores up wrath.
Sirach forbids postponing return to the Lord; Hebrews presses the present call of Today and warns against hardening through sin's deceit. Both oppose deferring the response to God.
Sirach denies benefit from unjust possessions in calamity; Ezekiel describes discarded silver and disregarded gold failing to satisfy lives, associated with torment for injustices.

Sirach pictures the double-tongued sinner walking every path; James calls the divided-minded person unstable in all his ways. Both portray instability through inconsistent direction; James' warning concerns doubting trust rather than explicitly deceptive speech.
Sirach calls for firm understanding and a single word; Jesus commands straightforward yes or no rather than additions from evil. Both demand dependable speech.
Sirach commands quick listening and a patient answer; James commands being quick to hear and slow to speak. The paired directions closely correspond.
Sirach tells the person without understanding to cover his mouth; Proverbs says one making himself mute will seem intelligent. Both commend silence over exposing one's lack of discernment.
Sirach places honor, dishonor and a person's fall in speech; Proverbs places death and life in the tongue's hand. Both emphasize speech's power over one's outcome.
Sirach condemns the whisperer who sets a verbal ambush and the double-tongued person; Proverbs contrasts a double-tongued man revealing plans in a council with a faithful person concealing matters.
Sirach warns against becoming an enemy in place of a friend and links this to double-tongued conduct; Proverbs' crooked, deceitful man separates friends.
Sirach warns that self-exaltation tears apart the soul; Proverbs places insolence before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall. Both present self-aggrandizement as destructive.
Sirach pictures self-destructive conduct as devoured leaves, lost fruit and a dry tree; Jeremiah contrasts the desert plant of misplaced trust with the fruitful tree trusting the Lord.
Sirach says an evil soul destroys its owner; Proverbs contrasts rescuing righteousness with lawless people caught in their own destruction. Both locate ruin in one's own moral condition.
Sirach warns against trusting a new friend quickly; chapter 12 says prosperity does not vindicate a friend and that even friends separate in adversity. The later warning supplies the test's reason.

Sirach's opportunistic friend fails in affliction; Proverbs contrasts wealth adding friends with a poor person abandoned even by his existing friend. Both expose friendship dependent on circumstances.
Sirach warns that a friend can turn to enmity and reproach; the psalm laments reproach from a familiar companion with whom the speaker formerly shared food and worship.
Sirach warns that a companion at table may fail in affliction; the psalm describes the trusted man who ate the speaker's bread becoming treacherous. Shared food proves no guarantee of loyalty.
Sirach's friend hides when his companion is brought low; Proverbs says the poor person is abandoned even by the friend he has. Both depict withdrawal precisely when help is needed.

Sirach commands separation from enemies before urging caution with friends; chapter 12 forbids trusting an enemy or stationing him beside oneself where he could displace the host. Both make distance from enemies a safeguard against hostile intentions.
Sirach calls the faithful friend a strong shelter; Proverbs calls for a friend at all times and brothers useful in need. Both value the security of enduring companionship.
Sirach denies an exchange price for a faithful friend; chapter 7 explicitly forbids trading a friend for profit or a true brother for gold.
The faithful friend as medicine for life develops verse 14's strong-shelter image. Both metaphors portray loyal friendship as preserving the recipient, rather than as a purchasable possession.
Sirach links one's own character and that of one's neighbor in rightly guided friendship; Proverbs says walking with the wise makes a person wise. Both connect character with companionship.
Sirach commends instruction from youth toward lifelong wisdom; Timothy is told to remain in learning grounded in sacred writings known from infancy, which can make him wise for salvation.

Sirach likens pursuing wisdom to cultivating and awaiting good fruit; James uses a farmer awaiting precious fruit to teach patience. The objects of waiting differ, while the agricultural comparison corresponds.

Sirach describes wisdom's severity for the uninstructed and the fainthearted person's failure to remain with her; Proverbs says the ungodly despise wisdom and discipline. Both depict resistance to instruction.

Wisdom feels like a testing stone discarded by the fainthearted; chapter 4 describes her first bringing fear and tormenting discipline while testing a person's soul. Both explain initial resistance to her training.
Sirach addresses a child and forbids rejecting counsel; Proverbs addresses children, calls for attention to a father's discipline, and forbids abandoning his law.
Sirach commands placing the neck in wisdom's collar; chapter 51 similarly commands placing the neck beneath a yoke to receive instruction. Both transform restraint into a learning metaphor.

Sirach urges willingly shouldering wisdom's bonds; Jesus invites hearers to take His yoke and learn from Him. Both picture willing submission to teaching as bearing a burden, without asserting identical speakers.

Sirach requires all one's soul and strength in pursuing wisdom; Deuteronomy requires love of God with all heart, soul and strength. The shared total-devotion language concerns wisdom and God respectively.
Sirach tells the pupil to trace out and seek wisdom until she is known; Proverbs compares seeking wisdom with searching for silver and treasures, leading to knowledge of God.
Sirach promises rest at the end of wisdom's discipline; Jesus promises rest for souls to those taking His yoke and learning from Him. The teaching-and-rest pattern is shared.

Wisdom's fetters become shelter and her collars become glory; chapter 4 likewise moves from fear and tormenting discipline to gladness and revelation. Both reverse the initial experience of her demands.
Sirach portrays wisdom as a robe of glory and a crown of rejoicing; Proverbs says wisdom will give the learner a crown of graces and delight. Both use crowning to describe her reward.

Sirach links willingness and giving one's soul to becoming instructed; Proverbs makes receiving the command and applying ear and heart conditions for understanding the fear of the Lord and finding knowledge of God.
Sirach promises wisdom to one who loves listening and inclines the ear; Proverbs says a wise hearer becomes wiser and the discerning gain guidance.
Sirach directs the learner to elders and wise companions; Job says wisdom belongs with much time and knowledge with a long life. Both acknowledge experience as a place to seek understanding.
Sirach commands attention to godly speech and proverbs of understanding; Proverbs names wise utterances, comparisons and riddles as things the discerning learner will understand.
Sirach urges repeated early visits to an understanding person's doors; Proverbs' Wisdom blesses the listener watching daily at her entrances. Both picture persistent attendance as pursuit of wisdom.
Sirach joins continuous meditation on the Lord's ordinances with receiving wisdom; the psalm's speaker attributes increased understanding to meditating on and seeking God's commandments.

The prohibition of evil and promise that evil will not overtake the reader is restated in verse 2 as withdrawal from injustice so it turns aside. The paired formulation reinforces the ethical cause and outcome.
Sirach commands withdrawal from injustice; Proverbs calls life's paths those turning aside from evils and says guarding one's ways preserves life. Both connect avoidance with protection.
Sirach warns against sowing injustice and reaping it sevenfold; Proverbs says sowing worthless things yields evils. Both use agricultural consequences to describe wrongdoing's return.
Sirach forbids seeking seats of leadership and royal glory; Proverbs forbids stationing oneself among rulers and warns against resulting humiliation. Both counsel restraint around high office.

Sirach forbids justifying oneself before the Lord; Jesus' parable contrasts the self-assured Pharisee with the penitent tax collector whom God justifies. The narrative illustrates the prohibition's danger.
Sirach warns that fear of a powerful person corrupts a judge's uprightness; Deuteronomy commands judges not to show partiality or shrink before a human face because judgment belongs to God.
Sirach forbids binding a sin twice and denies innocence even with one; chapter 5 likewise forbids adding sin upon sins through misplaced confidence about atonement.
Sirach rejects confidence that numerous gifts ensure divine acceptance; Isaiah rejects multiplied sacrifices and prayers from bloodstained hands and demands abandonment of evil and justice instead.
Sirach commands perseverance in prayer and almsgiving; Acts depicts Cornelius praying continually and giving many alms, both remembered before God.
Sirach forbids laughing at someone in bitterness of soul; Proverbs condemns laughing at the poor and rejoicing over someone perishing, relating that conduct to the Maker's response.
Sirach forbids devising a lie against brother or friend; Leviticus forbids lying and defrauding one's neighbor. Both prohibit deceit within personal relationships.
Sirach forbids willingness to tell any lie; Ephesians commands putting away falsehood and speaking truth to neighbors. Both reject deception as ordinary conduct.
Sirach warns against repeating a word in prayer; Jesus warns against babbling and supposing many words secure a hearing. Both challenge quantity of speech as a devotional advantage.

Sirach describes farming as work created by the Most High; Genesis places the man in God's garden to tend and keep it. The creation narrative gives a concrete instance of divinely appointed cultivation.
Sirach forbids counting oneself among a multitude of sinners; Proverbs warns against accepting the ungodly group's invitation or walking their path toward violence and plunder.
Sirach names fire and the worm as the ungodly's retribution; Isaiah depicts transgressors with undying worm and unquenched fire. The paired punishment images closely correspond.
Sirach forbids exchanging a friend or brother for profit or gold; chapter 6 says a faithful friend has no exchange price and his excellence cannot be measured by weight.

retained_triples_independently_read.relationship: A good wife exceeds material wealth
retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach values a wise, good wife's grace above gold; Proverbs values the courageous woman above costly stones. Both state that a worthy woman surpasses precious possessions.

Sirach forbids mistreating a faithful slave or dedicated hired worker; Colossians commands masters to provide slaves with justice and equity. Both impose duties upon those exercising household authority.

Sirach forbids depriving an understanding slave of freedom; Deuteronomy commands the Hebrew servant's seventh-year release with generous provision. The legal passage supplies a concrete release obligation, with its own stated scope.

Sirach commands attention to useful livestock; Proverbs commands knowing flocks' lives, tending herds and gathering fodder so sheep provide clothing. Both join husbandry to continued household provision.

Sirach commands discipline of children beginning in youth; Proverbs connects love for a son with careful discipline rather than withholding the staff. Both frame correction as a parental responsibility.
Sirach forbids dismissing a wife after one's heart; Paul forbids a brother dismissing an unbelieving wife willing to remain. Both require marital constancy, under different stated conditions.
Sirach commands wholehearted glory to a father and remembrance of a mother's labor; Exodus commands honoring father and mother. Both bind the child to both parents.
Sirach asks how one can repay the parents through whom one was born; First Timothy tells children and grandchildren to repay forebears through household care, particularly for a widow.

Sirach joins reverence for the Lord with honoring His priests; Deuteronomy grounds priestly dues in God's choosing them to minister and bless in His name. Their divine service explains the commanded regard.
Sirach commands love of the Maker and not abandoning His ministers; Deuteronomy specifically forbids forsaking the Levite throughout one's life in the land.

Sirach orders the priest's commanded portion, including shoulders and firstfruits; Deuteronomy specifies the foreleg and first produce as priestly dues. The lists overlap without being represented as identical.
Sirach connects an open hand to the poor with completed blessing; Deuteronomy commands generous giving to the needy and promises God's blessing upon the giver's work.

retained_triples_independently_read.relationship: Narrative illustration of kindness to the dead
retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach forbids withholding kindness from the dead; David calls burial of Saul and Jonathan an act of mercy and blesses those who performed it. Burial supplies a specific instance of that kindness.
Sirach commands mourning with those who mourn; Romans commands weeping with those who weep. Both require sharing another person's grief.
Sirach urges visiting a sick person; Jesus' judgment scene commends those who visited Him sick, explained as service to the least of His brothers. Both value personal presence with sufferers.

retained_triples_independently_read.relationship: Speech considered in light of mortality
retained_triples_independently_read.rationale: Sirach links remembering one's last things in every word with avoiding sin; the psalm joins guarding the tongue against sin with asking God to make one's limit and numbered days known.
Sirach warns against fighting a powerful person and falling into his hands; Proverbs likens a king's threat to a lion and says provoking him imperils one's life.

Sirach warns that a rich person's weight can overwhelm an opponent; Proverbs explicitly says the rich rule the poor. The connection concerns economic power, not an imported borrower-servant clause absent from this edition.
Sirach forbids adding wood to a talkative person's fire; Proverbs compares wood sustaining fire with an abusive man sustaining battle. Both use fuel imagery for escalating conflict.

Sirach forbids reproaching someone turning from sin and recalls shared liability; Galatians commands gentle restoration of one overtaken in transgression while remembering one's own vulnerability to temptation.
Sirach forbids dishonoring an elderly person; Leviticus commands rising before the grey-haired and honoring an elder. Both require respectful treatment of age.
Sirach forbids rejoicing over a dead person because all die; Ecclesiastes commends the house of mourning because death is every person's end and the living must take it to heart.

Sirach says wise discourse teaches understanding and service to high-ranking people; Daniel describes divinely given learning and understanding that distinguish the young men before the king and equip royal service.
Sirach values elders' discourse because they learned from their fathers; Deuteronomy commands remembering earlier generations and asking fathers and elders to recount them.
Sirach warns against kindling a sinner's coals and being burned; Proverbs joins coals and wood sustaining fire with an abusive person stirring battle. Both depict provocation through fire imagery.

Sirach warns that lending to someone stronger may mean losing the loan; chapter 29 describes borrowers delaying repayment, returning insults, and leaving lenders without their money. The later passage details the warned-of risk.
Sirach requires prospective guarantors to consider their ability to pay; Proverbs warns against pledging oneself when inability to pay may cost even one's bedding.
Sirach warns that a judge's prestige will influence a case in his favor; Deuteronomy forbids partiality and perverted judgment. The warning describes a danger the legal command condemns.

Sirach warns that a reckless travel companion's willfulness can endanger another; Proverbs forbids lodging with an angry friend lest his ways become snares for one's life. Both require caution about a companion's conduct.
Sirach forbids traveling with a hot-tempered person whose violence can kill where help is absent; Proverbs forbids companionship with a quick-tempered man lest his ways entangle one's life.
Sirach rejects counsel with a fool who cannot conceal a word; Proverbs contrasts a double-tongued revealer of plans with a faithful person who conceals matters.

Sirach warns against acting secretly before an unknown person; Micah warns against entrusting matters even to familiar companions. Both caution against exposing private matters to people whose reliability is not assured.

Sirach forbids revealing one's heart to every person; Micah warns against confidence in friends, leaders and a bed companion. The link concerns guarded trust, not an interpretation of Sirach's final favor clause.

source_only_deferrals_read.reason: The translator describes Israel receiving ancestral instructional writings. No target asserting an equivalent canon division or historical act was established; the prologue is preserved as its own source unit.
The translator identifies his grandfather Jesus and his reading of law and prophets. No identification with another scriptural Jesus or another author is assumed.
The grandfather's composition and intended readers are a particular historical authorship claim. No passage-grounded cross-reference to that act was established.
This unfinished appeal asks goodwill and forgiveness from readers and continues in the next unit. No distinct supported target for its particular editorial request was established.
The translator discusses loss of expressive force between Hebrew and another language. No linguistic equivalence or independent specialist verification is claimed.

The arrival under Euergetes in a thirty-eighth year is a specific historical notice. Its chronology and the expression about a likeness of learning were not independently identified with another passage.
Wakeful labor and publication for readers abroad describe this translator's work. No target narrating the same act or a specific enough literary correspondence was established.
This continuation states the translated work's goal of formation according to law. A generic obedience association was not retained for this particular editorial purpose.
